label: thm:buffered-main
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Buffered ERM

title: Proof
body_md:
For $t\ge0$, define the clean population and empirical threshold risks
\[
R_t(w):=\mathbb P\{M_q(w)\le t\},
\qquad
\widetilde R_t(w):=
\frac1Q\sum_{j=1}^Q\mathbf 1\{M_{q_j}(w)\le t\}.
\]
In particular, $\widetilde R_0$ is the ordinary empirical risk that would be available if the clean answer distributions were known.  It contains the randomness from sampling $Q$ questions, but not the finite-$N$ generation noise present in $\widehat R_{\varepsilon_N}$.  Write $\mathfrak v_Q=\mathfrak v_Q(\delta)$ for brevity.
The result follows from a chain of six inequalities.  By \cref{lem:clean-risk-deviation}, with probability at least $1-\delta/4$ over the sampled questions,
$|\widetilde R_t(w)-R_t(w)|\le\mathfrak v_Q$ simultaneously for all $w\inDelta_K$ and $t\in\{0,2\varepsilon_N\}$.  In particular,
\[
R_0(\widehat w_{\varepsilon_N}) \stackrel{(a)}{\le} \widetilde R_0(\widehat w_{\varepsilon_N})+\mathfrak v_Q, \quad \widetilde R_{2\varepsilon_N}(w^\star) \stackrel{(e)}{\le} R_{2\varepsilon_N}(w^\star)+\mathfrak v_Q.
\]

Separately, \cref{lem:margin-accuracy} shows, conditionally on the sampled questions, that event \eqref{eq:intro-uniform-event} holds with probability at least $1-\delta/4$ over the generations.  On this event, the buffered sandwich \eqref{eq:intro-sandwich} holds for every $w\inDelta_K$ and $j\in[Q]$.  Summing over $j$ and dividing by $Q$ gives
\[
\widetilde R_0(\widehat w_{\varepsilon_N}) \stackrel{(b)}{\le} \widehat R_{\varepsilon_N}(\widehat w_{\varepsilon_N}) \stackrel{(c)}{\le}  \widehat R_{\varepsilon_N}(w^\star) \stackrel{(d)}{\le} \widetilde R_{2\varepsilon_N}(w^\star).
\]
The middle inequality (c) follows from the minimality of $\widehat w_{\varepsilon_N}$ for the buffered empirical risk.  Finally, \cref{ass:one-sided-margin} gives
\[
R_{2\varepsilon_N}(w^\star)-R_0(w^\star)
=
\mathbb P\{0<M_q(w^\star)\le2\varepsilon_N\}
\stackrel{(f)}{\le} C_m(2\varepsilon_N)^beta.
\]
By a union bound, the two preceding events hold simultaneously with probability at least $1-\delta$.  Combining (a)--(f) in alphabetic order and using $R=R_0$ proves \eqref{eq:buffered-bound-exact}.

label: lem:weak-sign-patterns
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:weak-sign-patterns}
Fix affine functions $g_1,\dots,g_H:\mathbb R^p\to\mathbb R$.  Their weak sign patterns
are the vectors
\[
\bigl(\operatorname{sgn} g_1(x),\dots,\operatorname{sgn} g_H(x)\bigr)
\in\{-1,0,+1\}^H,
\qquad x\in\mathbb R^p.
\]
The number of distinct weak sign patterns is at most
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:faces-bound}
B(H,p):=\sum_{r=0}^{p}2^r\binom Hr.
\end{equation}
If $H\ge p\ge1$, then $B(H,p)\le(2eH/p)^p$.
If $H<p$, then $B(H,p)=3^H$.  In either case,
$\log B(H,p)\le Cp\log(eH)$ for a universal constant $C$.
head: environment
name: Weak sign patterns of affine functions

title: Proof
body_md:
Constant affine functions may be discarded because they do not increase
the number of patterns.  The hyperplanes $\{g_h=0\}$ partition $\mathbb R^p$
into relatively open faces of all dimensions.  The weak sign vector is
constant on each face, so it suffices to bound the total number of faces.

Let $F(H,p)$ be the largest possible number of such faces.  We prove the
bound by induction on $H$.  After arranging the first $H-1$ hyperplanes,
add the $H$th.  The preceding hyperplanes induce an arrangement of at
most $H-1$ hyperplanes on the new hyperplane, and hence at most
$F(H-1,p-1)$ faces there.  Each induced face can split one old face into
two while itself becoming a new face, producing a net increase of at
most two.  Therefore
\[
F(H,p)\le F(H-1,p)+2F(H-1,p-1),
\]
with $F(0,p)=F(H,0)=1$.  The quantity $B(H,p)$ obeys the same recurrence
by Pascal's identity, so induction proves $F(H,p)\le B(H,p)$.  Finally,
when $H\ge p$,
\[
B(H,p)
\le\sum_{r=0}^{p}\binom{2H}{r}
\le\left(\frac{2eH}{p}\right)^p.
\]
If $H<p$, then $\binom Hr=0$ for $r>H$, and the binomial theorem
gives $B(H,p)=\sum_{r=0}^H2^r\binom Hr=3^H$.  The stated logarithmic
bound follows from these two cases.

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $Z:=\sup_{h\in\mathcal H}|P_Qh-Ph|$.  Introduce an
independent ghost sample with empirical measure $P'_Q = \frac1Q \sum_{j=1}^Q \delta_{q'_j}$, and write
$Z':=\sup_{h\in\mathcal H}|P_Qh-P'_Qh|$.  Conditional on the original
sample, $P_Qh-Ph=\mathbb E[P_Qh-P'_Qh\mid q_1,\dots,q_Q]$ for every $h$.
Convexity of the supremum norm and of $x\mapsto e^{\lambda x}$ therefore
gives $\mathbb E e^{\lambda Z}\le\mathbb E e^{\lambda Z'}$ for every $\lambda>0$.

By exchangeability of each original--ghost pair, $Z'$ has the same
distribution after independent random swaps.  Encode the swaps by
Rademacher signs $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_Q$.  Conditional on the combined
sample, a fixed restriction of $h$ gives coefficients
$d_j=h(q_j)-h(q'_j)\in\{-1,0,+1\}$, and the randomized difference is
$Q^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^Q\sigma_jd_j$.  There are at most
$\Pi_{\mathcal H}(2Q)$ such restrictions.  Hoeffding's exponential-moment
bound, together with $e^{\lambda|x|}\le e^{\lambda x}+e^{-\lambda x}$,
thus gives
\[
\mathbb E e^{\lambda Z}
\le
2\Pi_{\mathcal H}(2Q)
\exp\left(\frac{\lambda^2}{2Q}\right).
\]
Markov's inequality with $\lambda=Qu$ now proves
\eqref{eq:vc-ineq}.

title: Proof
body_md:
We first bound the error of the deployment vote on questions with margin
greater than $r$.  The enlarged training buffer will then control the
population mass of the remaining questions.

Fix $w$ and $q$ with $M_q(w)>r$.  For each wrong answer
$a\ne a^\star(q)$, define the vote differences
\[
D_t(a):=\mathbf 1\{Y_t=a^\star(q)\}-\mathbf 1\{Y_t=a\},
\qquad t\in[T].
\]
Conditional on $q$, these variables are independent, take values in
$[-1,1]$, and have mean
$p_w(a^\star(q)\mid q)-p_w(a\mid q)\ge M_q(w)>r$.
Hoeffding's inequality gives
\[
\mathbb P\!\left\{\sum_{t=1}^T D_t(a)\le0\,\middle|\,q\right\}
\le e^{-T M_q(w)^2/2}
\le e^{-Tr^2/2}.
\]
The gold answer fails to be the unique empirical plurality only if this
event occurs for some wrong answer.  A union bound over at most $A-1$
wrong answers therefore gives the conditional error bound
$(A-1)e^{-Tr^2/2}$.  On questions with $M_q(w)\le r$, we bound the
conditional error probability by one.  Averaging over questions gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:deployment-vote-bound}
R_T^{\mathrm{dep}}(w)
\le R_r(w)+(A-1)e^{-Tr^2/2},
\qquad R_r(w):=\mathbb P\{M_q(w)\le r\}.
\end{equation}
This bound holds for every $w$.  Conditional on the training data, the
learned weight is fixed, and the fresh deployment question and generations
have the law used above.

The rest of the argument follows the proof of \cref{thm:buffered-main}, and we provide a brief sketch below.
Let $\widetilde R_s$ be the clean empirical threshold risk defined there.  Apply
\cref{lem:clean-risk-deviation} at the fixed thresholds $r$ and
$2\varepsilon_N+r$.  With probability at least $1-\delta/4$ over the questions,
$|\widetilde R_s(w)-R_s(w)|\le\mathfrak v_Q(\delta)$ simultaneously
for all $w$ and both thresholds.  Separately,
\cref{lem:margin-accuracy} bounds the uniform training-margin error by
$\varepsilon_N$ with probability at least $1-\delta/4$, conditional on the
questions.  On this latter event, the buffered sandwich
\eqref{eq:intro-sandwich}, with thresholds shifted by $r$, holds for every
$j\in[Q]$ and $w\inDelta_K$:
\[
\mathbf 1\{M_{q_j}(w)\le r\}
\le \mathbf 1\{\widehat M_{q_j}(w)\le\varepsilon_N+r\}
\le \mathbf 1\{M_{q_j}(w)\le2\varepsilon_N+r\}.
\]
Averaging over the training questions gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:deployment-buffer-sandwich}
\widetilde R_r(w)
\le \widehat R_{\varepsilon_N+r}(w)
\le \widetilde R_{2\varepsilon_N+r}(w),
\qquad w\inDelta_K.
\end{equation}
The two events hold jointly with probability at least $1-\delta$.
The same comparison argument now applies at these shifted thresholds:
the sandwich and empirical
optimality compare the clean empirical risks at
$\widehat w_{\varepsilon_N+r}$ and $w^\star$, while uniform convergence adds
$\mathfrak v_Q(\delta)$ at each end.  Consequently,
\[
R_r(\widehat w_{\varepsilon_N+r})
\le R_{2\varepsilon_N+r}(w^\star)+2\mathfrak v_Q(\delta).
\]
Since $2\varepsilon_N+r\le t_0$, the one-sided margin condition gives
\[
R_{2\varepsilon_N+r}(w^\star)-R(w^\star)
=\mathbb P\{0<M_q(w^\star)\le2\varepsilon_N+r\}
\le C_m(2\varepsilon_N+r)^beta.
\]
Combining this inequality with \eqref{eq:deployment-vote-bound} proves
\eqref{eq:finite-deployment-bound}.

For \eqref{eq:finite-deployment-rate}, take
$r_T=\sqrt{2/T}\log(eAT)$.  The last term in
\eqref{eq:finite-deployment-bound} becomes
$(A-1)\exp\{-\log^2(eAT)\}$, which, for fixed $A$, decreases faster than
any fixed power of $T^{-1}$.  Also,
\[
(2\varepsilon_N+r_T)^beta
\le C_beta(\varepsilon_N^beta+r_T^beta),
\qquad
r_T^beta=(2/T)^{beta/2}\log^beta(eAT).
\]
Here one can take $C_beta=3^beta$ for every $beta>0$, since
$2\varepsilon_N+r_T\le3\max\{\varepsilon_N,r_T\}$.
Substitution of \eqref{eq:epsilon-N} and \eqref{eq:vq} now gives
\eqref{eq:finite-deployment-rate}.

label: lem:margin-class-properties
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Basic properties of the margin class

title: Proof
body_md:
Convexity and reflection invariance are immediate from the definition of the class.  Since $[-1,1]$ is compact, the set of all probability measures on it is weakly compact.  It remains to show that the margin class is weakly closed.  Suppose $G_m\Rightarrow G$.  Fix $0<t<1$ and choose $\eta>0$ such that $t+\eta<1$.  By the Portmanteau theorem applied to the open interval $(-t-\eta,t+\eta)$,
\[
G([-t,t])
\le
G((-t-\eta,t+\eta))
\le
\liminf_{m\toinfinity}G_m((-t-\eta,t+\eta))
\le
L(t+\eta)^beta.
\]
Letting $\eta\downarrow0$ proves the margin inequality for $t<1$; at $t=1$ it is automatic because $G([-1,1])=1\le L$.  Thus $\mathcal G_{beta,L}$ is weakly closed and hence compact.  Taking $t\downarrow0$ shows that $G(\{0\})=0$.

For continuity of $theta$, let $\psi_\delta$ be the continuous clipped-sign function that equals $-1$ on $[-1,-\delta]$, equals $z/\delta$ on $[-\delta,\delta]$, and equals $1$ on $[\delta,1]$.  Uniformly over the margin class,
\[
\left|theta(G)-\int\psi_\delta\,\,\mathrm d G\right|
\le
2G([-\delta,\delta])
\le
2L\delta^beta.
\]
The integral of $\psi_\delta$ is weakly continuous.  First letting $m\toinfinity$ and then $\delta\downarrow0$ shows that $theta(G_m)\totheta(G)$.

Each coordinate of $K_nG$ is the integral of a bounded continuous polynomial in $z$, so the channel map is weakly continuous; both the channel and target maps are affine by linearity of integration.  Finally, reflection changes the sign of the target, and the Bernstein identity
\[
b_{k,n}\!\left(\frac{1-z}{2}\right)
=
b_{n-k,n}\!\left(\frac{1+z}{2}\right)
\]
gives the channel identity in \eqref{eq:reflection-properties}.

label: eq:abstract-diameter-delta
title: Proof
body_md:
Let
\[
\tau_-:=\min_{(p,\tau)\in\mathcal X}\tau,
\qquad
\tau_+:=\max_{(p,\tau)\in\mathcal X}\tau,
\qquad
D:=\tau_+-\tau_-.
\]
Because all categorical laws are within Hellinger distance $\sqrt2$, we have $D=omega_{\mathcal X}(\sqrt2)$.  Set
\[
A:=32,
\qquad
\varepsilon_0:=\frac{A}{\sqrt Q},
\qquad
\delta:=omega_{\mathcal X}(\varepsilon_0).
\]
Our goal is to show an estimator that has expected absolute error at most $7\delta/2$, uniformly over $\mathcal X$.
If $D=0$, the target is constant, and the corresponding constant estimator achieves zero error.  If $\varepsilon_0\ge\sqrt2$, then $\delta=D$, and the midpoint of $[\tau_-,\tau_+]$ has error at most
$D/2 = \delta/2$.
We may therefore assume $\varepsilon_0<\sqrt2$.  The scaling lemma gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:abstract-diameter-delta}
D
\le
\frac{2\delta}{\varepsilon_0^2}.
\end{equation}
In particular, $\delta=0$ would imply $D=0$.  If $\delta\ge D/6$, the midpoint again has error at most $D/2\le3\delta$.  It remains to consider
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:nontrivial-search-case}
0<\delta<D/6,
\end{equation}
which, together with \eqref{eq:abstract-diameter-delta}, implies $Q>3A^2$.

We now construct a sample-split interval-search estimator.  It proceeds through stages $s=0,\dots,S-1$ and maintains a nested sequence of intervals $I_s$ intended to localize $\tau$.  Start from $I_0=[\tau_-,\tau_+]$.  The observations are divided into $S$ disjoint blocks, one per stage, with block sizes specified below.  At stage $s$, write $I_s=[a_s,b_s]$ and $\ell_s=b_s-a_s$.  Using only block $s$, test the lower third of $I_s$ against the upper third through the composite hypotheses
\[
H_{s}^-:\ \tau\le a_s+\frac{\ell_s}{3}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
H_{s}^+:\ \tau\ge a_s+\frac{2\ell_s}{3}.
\]
If the test chooses $H_{s}^-$, retain the lower two thirds, $I_{s+1}=[a_s,a_s+2\ell_s/3]$; if it chooses $H_{s}^+$, retain the upper two thirds, $I_{s+1}=[a_s+\ell_s/3,b_s]$.  The two candidate intervals overlap in the middle third of $I_s$.  Thus, when $\tau$ lies in that middle third, either test outcome retains it.

The interval lengths are deterministic and satisfy
\[
\ell_s=\left(\frac23\right)^sD.
\]
Stop at the first integer $S$ for which $\ell_S\le6\delta$, and return the midpoint $\widehat\tau$ of $I_S$.  It remains to choose the stagewise tests and block sizes.  For $s<S$, define
\[
g_s:=\frac{\ell_s}{3},
\qquad
r_s^2:=\frac{\varepsilon_0^2\ell_s}{6\delta},
\qquad
u_s:=\frac{\ell_s}{\delta}>6.
\]
Here $g_s$ is the separation between the two outer thirds, while $u_s$ measures the current interval length in units of the target accuracy $\delta$.  Since $\ell_s>6\delta$, we have $r_s\ge\varepsilon_0$, while \eqref{eq:abstract-diameter-delta} gives $r_s^2\le1/3<2$.  Thus $\varepsilon_0\le r_s<\sqrt2$, and \cref{lem:modulus-scaling}, applied at radii $\varepsilon_0$ and $r_s$, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:search-separation}
omega_{\mathcal X}(r_s)
\le
\left(\frac{r_s}{\varepsilon_0}\right)^2\delta
=
\frac{\ell_s}{6}
=\frac{g_s}{2}
<g_s.
\end{equation}

For every possible interval $I_s$, the observation laws $p$ generated under $H_s^-$ and $H_s^+$ form two compact convex sets.  Indeed, each is the image, under the coordinate projection $(p,\tau)\mapsto p$, of the intersection of $\mathcal X$ with the corresponding closed halfspace.
By \eqref{eq:search-separation}, every pair across these sets is separated by more than $r_s$ in Hellinger distance.  If either set is empty, use the corresponding deterministic decision.  Otherwise, apply the test supplied by \cref{lem:robust-affinity-test} using a fresh block of
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:search-allocation}
k_s
:=
\left\lceil
\frac{4}{r_s^2}\log u_s
\right\rceil
\end{equation}
observations.

The use of a fresh block makes the testing guarantee valid conditional on the preceding outcomes.  Let $\mathcal F_s$ be the sigma-field generated by blocks $0,\dots,s-1$ and any auxiliary randomization used through stage $s-1$, so that $I_s$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable.  Call the update at stage $s$ \emph{unsafe} if $I_{s+1}$ does not contain $\tau$, and let $A_s$ be the event that all preceding updates are safe.  Since $I_0$ contains $\tau$ and the intervals are nested, $A_s=\{\tau\in I_s\}$.  On $A_s$, either $\tau$ lies in the middle third, in which case an unsafe update is impossible, or the true law $p$ belongs to one of the two tested composite hypotheses.  Since block $s$ is independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and has law $p^{\otimes k_s}$ conditional on that history, the robust test bound gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:search-stage-error}
\mathbb P_p(\tau\notin I_{s+1}\mid\mathcal F_s)
\le
\exp\left(-\frac{k_s r_s^2}{2}\right)
\le
u_s^{-2}
=
\left(\frac{\delta}{\ell_s}\right)^2
\qquad\text{on }A_s.
\end{equation}

We now bound the risk of this estimator.  Let $E_s:=A_s\cap\{\tau\notin I_{s+1}\}$ be the event that the first unsafe update occurs at stage $s$.  If no update is unsafe, then $\tau\in I_S$ and $|\widehat\tau-\tau|\le\ell_S/2\le3\delta$.  On $E_s$, all preceding updates were safe, so $\tau\in I_s$ immediately before the unsafe update.  Every later interval, and hence $\widehat\tau$, remains inside $I_s$; therefore the loss on $E_s$ is at most $\ell_s$.  Moreover, \eqref{eq:search-stage-error} gives
\[
\mathbb P_p(E_s)
=
\mathbb E_p\left[
\mathbf 1_{A_s}
\mathbb P_p\{\tau\notin I_{s+1}\mid\mathcal F_s\}
\right]
\le
\left(\frac{\delta}{\ell_s}\right)^2.
\]
The events $E_s$ are disjoint, and consequently
\begin{align*}
\sup_{(p,\tau)\in\mathcal X}
\mathbb E_p|\widehat\tau-\tau|
&\le
3\delta
+
\sum_{s=0}^{S-1}
\ell_s\left(\frac{\delta}{\ell_s}\right)^2.
\end{align*}
Finally, $\ell_{S-1}>6\delta$ and the interval lengths form a geometric sequence, so
\[
\sum_{s=0}^{S-1}\frac1{\ell_s}
\le
\frac1{\ell_{S-1}}
\sum_{j=0}^infinity\left(\frac23\right)^j
<\frac1{2\delta}.
\]
Thus the expected loss is at most $7\delta/2$.

It remains to verify that the planned independent blocks fit within the original sample.  From \eqref{eq:search-allocation},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:allocation-sum-start}
\sum_{s=0}^{S-1}k_s
\le
S+\frac{24Q}{A^2}
\sum_{s=0}^{S-1}\frac{\log u_s}{u_s}.
\end{equation}
Minimality of $S$ gives $6<u_{S-1}\le9$.  Writing $j=S-1-s$, we have $u_s=u_{S-1}(3/2)^j$, and hence
\begin{align}
\sum_{s=0}^{S-1}\frac{\log u_s}{u_s}
 \le
\frac16\sum_{j=0}^infinity
\left(\frac23\right)^j
\left[\log9+j\log\left(\frac32\right)\right]
=
\log\left(\frac92\right).
\label{eq:allocation-geometric-sum}
\end{align}
Also,
\[
S
\le
1+\log_{3/2}\left(\frac{D}{6\delta}\right)
\le
1+\frac{D}{2\delta}
\le
1+\frac{Q}{A^2},
\]
where the second inequality uses $\log_{3/2}x\le3x$ for $x\ge1$.  Combining this with \cref{eq:allocation-sum-start,eq:allocation-geometric-sum} gives
\[
\sum_{s=0}^{S-1}k_s
\le
1+\frac{Q}{A^2}
+\frac{24Q}{A^2}\log\left(\frac92\right)
<Q,
\]
using $A=32$ and $Q>3A^2$.  Any unused observations are ignored.  The estimator is therefore feasible with $Q$ observations, which completes the proof of \eqref{eq:modulus-upper}.

title: Proof
body_md:
By \cref{lem:margin-class-properties}, the set
\[
\mathcal X_n
:=
\{(K_nG,theta(G)):G\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}\}
\subsetDelta_{n+1}\times[-1,1]
\]
is compact and convex, and both coordinates are continuous affine functions of $G$.  Its indirect modulus is exactly \eqref{eq:modulus}.  Applying \cref{thm:modulus-upper} with $\mathcal X=\mathcal X_n$, followed by \cref{lem:modulus-scaling}, gives
\[
\mathcal R^{\mathrm{abs}}_{Q,n}(beta,L)
\le
C\,omega_{n,beta,L}(Q^{-1/2})
\]
for a universal constant $C$.  This proves the rightmost inequality in \eqref{eq:scalar-modulus-chain}; the pointwise reduction \eqref{eq:dec-le-abs} gives the middle inequality.

It remains to prove the lower bound for decision regret.  Fix  $\varepsilon=(2\sqrt Q)^{-1}$
and take any $G,H\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}$ satisfying $h(K_nG,K_nH)\le\varepsilon$.  After interchanging $G$ and $H$ if necessary, write
\[
\delta:=theta(G)-theta(H)\ge0.
\]
The original targets may have the same sign, in which case the same side is optimal under both distributions and the pair need not be difficult for the decision problem.  Reflection symmetrization produces a pair with opposite optimal decisions.  Specifically, define
\[
G_+:=\frac12(G+H^\dagger),
\qquad
G_-:=\frac12(H+G^\dagger).
\]
By \cref{lem:margin-class-properties}, $G_+,G_-\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}$ and
\[
theta(G_+)=\frac\delta2,
\qquad
theta(G_-)=-\frac\delta2.
\]
Writing $P_+=K_nG_+$ and $P_-=K_nG_-$, joint convexity of squared Hellinger distance and invariance under reversal of the count labels give
\begin{align}
h^2(P_+,P_-)
&\le
\frac12h^2(K_nG,K_nH)
+
\frac12h^2(K_nH^\dagger,K_nG^\dagger)
\notag\\
&=
h^2(K_nG,K_nH)
\le\varepsilon^2.
\label{eq:symmetrized-hellinger}
\end{align}

For probability measures $P$ and $R$, write
\[
\rho(P,R):=\sum_x\sqrt{P(x)R(x)}
=1-\frac12h^2(P,R)
\]
for their Hellinger affinity.  Affinity factorizes over product measures, so
\begin{align}
h^2(P^{\otimes Q},R^{\otimes Q})
&=
2\{1-\rho(P,R)^Q\}\notag\\
&=
2\left\{1-\left(1-\frac12h^2(P,R)\right)^Q\right\}
\le
Qh^2(P,R).
\label{eq:product-hellinger}
\end{align}
The last inequality is Bernoulli's inequality.  Under the present Hellinger convention, Cauchy--Schwarz also gives
\begin{align}
\operatorname{TV}(P,R)
&=
\frac12\sum_x
|\sqrt{P(x)}-\sqrt{R(x)}|
(\sqrt{P(x)}+\sqrt{R(x)})\notag\\
&\le
h(P,R)\sqrt{1-\frac14h^2(P,R)}
\le h(P,R).
\label{eq:TV-le-hellinger}
\end{align}
Combining \eqref{eq:symmetrized-hellinger}--\eqref{eq:TV-le-hellinger} with $\varepsilon=(2\sqrt Q)^{-1}$ yields
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:product-TV-small}
\operatorname{TV}(P_+^{\otimes Q},P_-^{\otimes Q})
\le\frac12.
\end{equation}

Now fix any, possibly randomized, decision rule $\widehat\sigma$.  Because a wrong decision costs $\delta/2$ under either $G_+$ or $G_-$ (recall \eqref{eq:scalar-decision-loss}),
\begin{align}
\sup_{F\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}}
\mathbb E_F\mathcal L_F(\widehat\sigma)
&\ge
\frac12\left\{
\mathbb E_{G_+}\mathcal L_{G_+}(\widehat\sigma)
+
\mathbb E_{G_-}\mathcal L_{G_-}(\widehat\sigma)
\right\}\notag\\
&=
\frac\delta4\left\{
P_+^{\otimes Q}(\widehat\sigma=-1)
+
P_-^{\otimes Q}(\widehat\sigma=+1)
\right\}\notag\\
&\ge
\frac\delta4
\left\{1-\operatorname{TV}(P_+^{\otimes Q},P_-^{\otimes Q})\right\}
\ge
\frac\delta8.
\label{eq:decision-le-cam}
\end{align}
The penultimate inequality is Le Cam's two-point inequality.  Since \eqref{eq:decision-le-cam} holds for every admissible pair $G,H$ and every decision rule, taking first the infimum over $\widehat\sigma$ and then the supremum over all pairs in the definition of the modulus gives
\[
\mathcal R^{\mathrm{dec}}_{Q,n}(beta,L)
\ge
\frac18\,
omega_{n,beta,L}\!\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt Q}\right).
\]
Finally, \cref{lem:modulus-scaling} gives
\[
omega_{n,beta,L}\!\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt Q}\right)
\ge
\frac14omega_{n,beta,L}(Q^{-1/2}),
\]
which proves the lower bound in \eqref{eq:scalar-modulus-chain}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider the fixed family
\[
\mathfrak G_beta
:=
\{G_{\sigma,m}:\sigma\in\{-1,+1\},\ 0<m\le1/2\},
\qquad
G_{\sigma,m}
=
\frac{1-m^beta}{2}(\delta_{-1}+\delta_{+1})
+m^beta\delta_{\sigma m}.
\]
For $0<t<m$ there is no mass in $[-t,t]$, while for $m\le t<1$ the mass is $m^beta\le t^beta$.  Hence the family lies in $\mathcal G_{beta,L}$, independently of $Q,n$, and $theta(G_{\sigma,m})=\sigma m^beta$.

Let $P_{\sigma,m}=K_nG_{\sigma,m}$.  Augmenting the observation by revealing whether the latent draw came from the central component and then applying data processing gives
\[
\operatorname{KL}(P_{+1,m}\|P_{-1,m})
\le
m^beta
\operatorname{KL}\!\left(
\operatorname{Bin}\left(n,\frac{1+m}{2}\right)
\middle\|
\operatorname{Bin}\left(n,\frac{1-m}{2}\right)
\right)
\le 4nm^{beta+2},
\]
where the last inequality uses
\[
\operatorname{KL}\!\left(
\operatorname{Ber}\left(\frac{1+m}{2}\right)
\middle\|
\operatorname{Ber}\left(\frac{1-m}{2}\right)
\right)
=
m\log\frac{1+m}{1-m}
\le4m^2
\]
for $m\le1/2$.  Since squared Hellinger distance is bounded by Kullback--Leibler divergence, taking
\[
m
=
\left(\frac{\varepsilon^2}{16n}\right)^{1/(beta+2)}
\]
for $\varepsilon\le c_0(beta)$ ensures both $m\le1/2$ and $h(P_{+1,m},P_{-1,m})\le\varepsilon$.  Meanwhile,
\[
|theta(G_{+1,m})-theta(G_{-1,m})|
=2m^beta
\asymp_beta
\left(\frac{\varepsilon^2}{n}\right)^{beta/(beta+2)}.
\]
This proves \eqref{eq:pooled-modulus-lower}.  Its minimax consequence follows from \cref{thm:scalar-modulus}, monotonicity of the modulus, and a fixed reduction of the constant multiplying $Q^{-1/2}$ when necessary.

body_md:
Let $(Z,S,\widehat\xi)$ denote a generic copy of $(Z_j,S_j,\widehat\xi_j)$, where $\widehat\xi=\mathbf 1\{S>n/2\}-\mathbf 1\{S<n/2\}$.  Then $\mathbb E_G\widehattheta_{\mathrm{plug}}=\mathbb E_G\widehat\xi$, and the bias--fluctuation decomposition gives
\[
\mathbb E_G|\widehattheta_{\mathrm{plug}}-theta(G)|
\le
|\mathbb E_G\widehat\xi-theta(G)|
+
\mathbb E_G|\widehattheta_{\mathrm{plug}}-\mathbb E_G\widehattheta_{\mathrm{plug}}|.
\]
Because the $\widehat\xi_j$ are iid and bounded by one, the fluctuation term satisfies
\[
\mathbb E_G|\widehattheta_{\mathrm{plug}}-\mathbb E_G\widehattheta_{\mathrm{plug}}|
\le
\sqrt{\operatorname{Var}_G(\widehattheta_{\mathrm{plug}})}
\le
Q^{-1/2}.
\]

It remains to control the bias.  The margin condition implies $G(\{0\})=0$, so the value of $\operatorname{sgn}$ at zero is immaterial.  For $Z\ne0$, the pointwise inequality $|\widehat\xi-\operatorname{sgn}(Z)|\le2\mathbf 1\{\widehat\xi\ne\operatorname{sgn}(Z)\}$ gives
\begin{align*}
|\mathbb E_G\widehat\xi-theta(G)|
&\le
\mathbb E_G\bigl|\mathbb E[\widehat\xi\mid Z]-\operatorname{sgn}(Z)\bigr|\\
&\le
\mathbb E_G\mathbb E\bigl[|\widehat\xi-\operatorname{sgn}(Z)|\mid Z\bigr]\\
&\le
2\,\mathbb E_G\mathbb P\{\widehat\xi\ne\operatorname{sgn}(Z)\mid Z\}.
\end{align*}
For $z\ne0$, conditional Hoeffding bounds the probability of an incorrect sign or a tie by
\[
\mathbb P_z\{\widehat\xi\ne\operatorname{sgn}(z)\}
\le
e^{-nz^2/2}.
\]
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:plugin-bias-preintegration}
|\mathbb E_G\widehat\xi-theta(G)|
\le
2\,\mathbb E_Ge^{-nZ^2/2}.
\end{equation}

To integrate this bound, put $a=n^{-1/2}$ and split the range of $|Z|$ into
\[
A_{-1}:=\{z\in[-1,1]:|z|\le a\},
\qquad
A_j:=\{z\in[-1,1]:2^ja<|z|\le2^{j+1}a\},
\quad j\ge0.
\]
The margin condition, together with the trivial probability bound once $2^{j+1}a>1$, gives
\[
G(A_{-1})\le Ln^{-beta/2},
\qquad
G(A_j)\le L2^{(j+1)beta}n^{-beta/2}.
\]
On $A_j$, one has $e^{-nZ^2/2}\le e^{-2^{2j-1}}$.  Therefore
\begin{align*}
\mathbb E_Ge^{-nZ^2/2}
&\le
Ln^{-beta/2}
\left[
1+2^beta\sum_{j\ge0}2^{jbeta}e^{-2^{2j-1}}
\right]
\;\le
C_{beta,L}n^{-beta/2},
\end{align*}
because the series converges.  Combining this estimate with \eqref{eq:plugin-bias-preintegration} and the fluctuation bound proves \eqref{eq:plugin-scalar}.  Finally, \eqref{eq:pointwise-decision-reduction} gives the same upper bound for the regret of $\widehat\sigma_{\mathrm{plug}}$.

For every $G\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}$ and every integer $M\ge1$, there is an equal-weight measure
\[
G^{(M)}
=
\frac1M\sum_{r=1}^M\delta_{z_r}
\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}
\]
such that
\[
|theta(G^{(M)})-theta(G)|\le M^{-1},
\qquad
G^{(M)}\Rightarrow G
\quad\text{as }M\toinfinity.
\]
Consequently, for every fixed $n$,
\[
\operatorname{TV}(K_nG^{(M)},K_nG)\to0.
\]
If $H$ is the reflection of $G$ under $z\mapsto-z$, the approximations may be chosen so that $H^{(M)}$ is the reflection of $G^{(M)}$.

name: Equal-weight discretization preserving the margin class

title: Proof
body_md:
Because $G\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}$, $G(\{0\})=0$.  Write
\[
p_+=G((0,1]),
\qquad
p_-=G([-1,0)),
\qquad
p_++p_-=1,
\]
and define the one-sided small-ball functions
\[
F_+(t)=G((0,t]),
\qquad
F_-(t)=G([-t,0)),
\qquad 0<t\le1.
\]

The construction treats the two sides of zero separately.  Starting at
zero, divide as much of the mass on each side as possible into blocks of
mass $1/M$, and replace each block by an atom at its endpoint farther from
zero.  Any atom needed to round the number of blocks is placed at $+1$ or
$-1$.  Moving mass outward in this way is what preserves the margin bound.

To make this precise, choose an integer $m_+$ nearest to $Mp_+$ and put
$m_-=M-m_+$.  These are the numbers of atoms assigned to the positive and
negative sides.  They satisfy
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:side-mass-rounding}
\left|\frac{m_+}{M}-p_+\right|\le\frac1{2M},
\qquad
\left|\frac{m_-}{M}-p_-\right|\le\frac1{2M}.
\end{equation}
Let
\[
k_+=\lfloor Mp_+\rfloor,
\qquad
k_-=\lfloor Mp_-\rfloor,
\qquad
e_+=m_+-k_+,
\qquad
e_-=m_--k_-.
\]
Here $k_\pm$ count the complete mass-$1/M$ blocks and $e_\pm$ account for
the possible rounding atom.  Since $Mp_++Mp_-=M$, we have
$e_+,e_-\in\{0,1\}$ and $e_++e_-\in\{0,1\}$.  For
$j=1,\dots,k_+$ and $j=1,\dots,k_-$, respectively, define the outward
quantiles
\[
x_j^+
=
\inf\{t\in(0,1]:F_+(t)\ge j/M\},
\qquad
x_j^-
=
\inf\{t\in(0,1]:F_-(t)\ge j/M\}.
\]
Thus $x_j^+$ and $-x_j^-$ are the endpoints farther from zero of the
$j$th cumulative blocks on the two sides.  Set
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:outward-quantile-measure}
G^{(M)}
=
\frac1M
\left\{
\sum_{j=1}^{k_+}\delta_{x_j^+}
+
\sum_{j=1}^{k_-}\delta_{-x_j^-}
+
e_+\delta_{+1}
+
e_-\delta_{-1}
\right\}.
\end{equation}
For $0<t<1$, the generalized-inverse property gives
$x_j^+\le t$ if and only if $j/M\le F_+(t)$.  Consequently,
$\#\{j:x_j^+\le t\}=\lfloor MF_+(t)\rfloor$; the same argument applies
on the negative side.  Because the possible extra atoms at $\pm1$ are not
counted, we obtain
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:outward-quantile-subdistributions}
G^{(M)}((0,t])
=
\frac{\lfloor MF_+(t)\rfloor}{M},
\qquad
G^{(M)}([-t,0))
=
\frac{\lfloor MF_-(t)\rfloor}{M}.
\end{equation}
In particular, the discretization places no more mass near zero than the
original distribution:
\[
G^{(M)}([-t,t])
\le
F_+(t)+F_-(t)
=
G([-t,t])
\le
Lt^beta.
\]
At $t=1$, the required inequality is $1\le L$.  Hence $G^{(M)}\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}$ with exactly the same margin constant.

The positive mass of $G^{(M)}$ is $m_+/M$, so \eqref{eq:side-mass-rounding} gives
\[
|theta(G^{(M)})-theta(G)|
=
2\left|\frac{m_+}{M}-p_+\right|
\le M^{-1}.
\]
Equation~\eqref{eq:outward-quantile-subdistributions} shows directly that,
for every $0<t<1$,
\[
0\le F_+(t)-G^{(M)}((0,t])<\frac1M,
\qquad
0\le F_-(t)-G^{(M)}([-t,0))<\frac1M.
\]
At $t=1$, the corresponding errors are at most $1/(2M)$ by
\eqref{eq:side-mass-rounding}.  Thus the one-sided distribution functions
of $G^{(M)}$ converge to those of $G$, which implies
$G^{(M)}\Rightarrow G$.  Each coordinate of $K_nG^{(M)}$ is the
integral of a bounded continuous polynomial in $z$, so weak convergence
implies that $K_nG^{(M)}$ converges coordinatewise to $K_nG$.  Since the
output alphabet is finite, this implies
\[
\operatorname{TV}(K_nG^{(M)},K_nG)\to0.
\]
Finally, if $H$ is the reflection of $G$, define $H^{(M)}$ to be the reflection of $G^{(M)}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $Q>M$, the right side of \eqref{eq:permutation-TV} is at least one and the claim is trivial.  Assume henceforth that $Q\le M$.

We compare two joint laws on the common augmented variables
$(q,R,J,S)=((q_j,R_j,J_j,S_j))_{j=1}^Q$.  Under the
\emph{permutation law}, first draw $R_1,\dots,R_Q$ iid uniformly from
$[M]$ and, conditional on $R$, draw the $q_j$ independently and uniformly
within $I_{R_j}$.  Independently draw a uniform permutation $\Pi$ of
$[M]$, set $J_j=\Pi(R_j)$, and then draw the counts conditionally
independently according to
\[
S_j\mid J_j
\sim
\operatorname{Bin}\!\left(n,\frac{1+z_{J_j}}2\right).
\]
This construction generates $q_1,\dots,q_Q\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
\lambda$, and its $(q,S)$-marginal is
$\overline{\mathbb P}^{Q,n}_{G_M,M}$.

Under the \emph{iid law}, generate $(R,q)$ in the same way, but draw
$J_1,\dots,J_Q$ iid uniformly from $[M]$, independently of $(R,q)$, and
then use the same conditional distribution of $S$ given $J$.  Its
$(q,S)$-marginal is
$\lambda^{\otimes Q}\otimes(K_nG_M)^{\otimes Q}$.  Since projection onto
$(q,S)$ cannot increase total variation, it is enough to compare these
two augmented laws.

Let
\[
\mathcal D_{Q,M}
:=
\{(r_1,\dots,r_Q)\in[M]^Q:r_1,\dots,r_Q\text{ are distinct}\}.
\]
The uniform law on $\mathcal D_{Q,M}$ is exactly the law obtained by
drawing $Q$ labels uniformly without replacement from $[M]$, with the
$j$th coordinate recording the label drawn for observation $j$.

Let $A:=\{R\in\mathcal D_{Q,M}\}$ under the permutation law.  Conditional
on $A$, the vector $R$ is uniform on $\mathcal D_{Q,M}$.  For every fixed
$r\in\mathcal D_{Q,M}$, the vector
$\Pi(r):=(\Pi(r_1),\dots,\Pi(r_Q))$ is also uniform on
$\mathcal D_{Q,M}$, and its distribution does not depend on $r$.
Consequently, under the permutation law conditional on $A$, the vectors
$R$ and $J$ are independent and each is uniform on
$\mathcal D_{Q,M}$.

Under the iid law, let
$E:=\{R\in\mathcal D_{Q,M},\ J\in\mathcal D_{Q,M}\}$.  Since $R$ and $J$
are independent and each has iid uniform coordinates before conditioning,
conditional on $E$ they remain independent and each is uniform on
$\mathcal D_{Q,M}$.  Given $(R,J)$, both laws draw $q_j$ uniformly within
$I_{R_j}$ and generate $S_j$ through the same binomial channel indexed by
$J_j$.  Hence their conditional laws agree exactly:
\[
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{perm}}(q,R,J,S\mid A)
=
\mathcal L_{\mathrm{iid}}(q,R,J,S\mid E).
\]

The probability of a collision in one iid sample of $Q$ indices is
\[
\alpha_{Q,M}
=
1-\frac{(M)_Q}{M^Q}
\le
\binom Q2\frac1M.
\]
Using the elementary inequality $\operatorname{TV}(P,P(\cdot\mid B))\le P(B^c)$ and the triangle inequality,
\begin{align*}
\operatorname{TV}(\mathcal L_{\mathrm{perm}}(q,R,J,S),
     \mathcal L_{\mathrm{iid}}(q,R,J,S))
&\le
\mathbb P_{\mathrm{perm}}(A^c)
+
\mathbb P_{\mathrm{iid}}(E^c)\\
&=
\alpha_{Q,M}
+
\{1-(1-\alpha_{Q,M})^2\}\\
&\le3\alpha_{Q,M}.
\end{align*}
Projecting both augmented laws onto $(q,S)$ now proves
\eqref{eq:permutation-TV}.

title: Proof
body_md:
The upper inequality is \eqref{eq:obs-le-count}.  We prove the lower inequality.

We first record the Bayes reduction that guides the construction.  Suppose
$\nu_+$ and $\nu_-$ are finitely supported priors on
$\mathfrak Z_{beta,L}$ such that, for some $b>0$,
$theta_Z=\pm b$ for every $Z\in\operatorname{supp}(\nu_\pm)$,
respectively.  Let $\overline{\mathbb P}_+$ and
$\overline{\mathbb P}_-$ denote the corresponding prior-averaged laws of
the full observed sample.  Then every decision rule $\widehat\sigma$
satisfies
\begin{align}
\sup_{Z\in\mathfrak Z_{beta,L}}
\mathbb E_Z\mathcal L_Z(\widehat\sigma)
&\ge
\frac b2
\left\{
\overline{\mathbb P}_+(\widehat\sigma=-1)
+
\overline{\mathbb P}_-(\widehat\sigma=+1)
\right\}\notag\\
&\ge
\frac b2
\left\{1-\operatorname{TV}(\overline{\mathbb P}_+,\overline{\mathbb P}_-)\right\}.
\label{eq:transfer-bayes-reduction}
\end{align}
The first inequality bounds the maximum risk below by its average under
the prior that first chooses the sign uniformly and then draws $Z$ from
the corresponding $\nu_\pm$; the second is the usual two-point
testing inequality.  It therefore suffices to construct two such priors
with $b$ comparable to the modulus and whose prior-averaged data laws
have total variation bounded away from one.

Fix $\varepsilon_Q:=(64\sqrt Q)^{-1}$ and take any
$0<Delta<omega_{n,beta,L}(\varepsilon_Q)$.  By the reflection
symmetrization used in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:scalar-modulus},
there exist $G_+,G_-\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:transfer-hard-pair}
G_-=G_+^\dagger,
\qquad
theta(G_+)=a,
\qquad
theta(G_-)=-a,
\qquad
a>Delta/2,
\qquad
h(K_nG_+,K_nG_-)\le\varepsilon_Q,
\end{equation}
where $\dagger$ denotes reflection under $z\mapsto-z$.

Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:equal-weight-discretization} to $G_+$ and reflect the
result to obtain equal-weight measures $G^{(M)}_+$ and $G^{(M)}_-$.  Write
\[
P^{(M)}_\pm:=K_nG^{(M)}_\pm,
\qquad
a_M:=theta(G^{(M)}_+).
\]
Because the targets and channel laws converge, and because $M$ may be
taken arbitrarily large, choose $M$ so that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:transfer-M-choices}
a_M\geDelta/4,
\qquad
h(P^{(M)}_+,K_nG_+)\le\varepsilon_Q,
\qquad
6\alpha_{Q,M}\le\frac18.
\end{equation}
Reflection gives the analogous channel bound for the negative hypothesis
and $theta(G^{(M)}_-)=-theta(G^{(M)}_+)$.  The triangle inequality gives
\[
h(P^{(M)}_+,P^{(M)}_-)
\le3\varepsilon_Q.
\]
Consequently, the product-Hellinger and total-variation inequalities
\eqref{eq:product-hellinger} and \eqref{eq:TV-le-hellinger} give
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:transfer-product-TV}
\operatorname{TV}\!\left(
(P^{(M)}_+)^{\otimes Q},
(P^{(M)}_-)^{\otimes Q}
\right)
\le
\frac{3}{64}.
\end{equation}

Each discretized alternative is now lifted to a family of deterministic
question-to-advantage maps.  For each sign, let $\nu_\pm$ be the uniform
permutation prior from Lemma~\ref{lem:permutation-embedding}, constructed
using $G^{(M)}_\pm$.  Every map in the support of $\nu_\pm$ belongs to
$\mathfrak Z_{beta,L}$ and has target $\pm a_M$.  Denote the corresponding
prior-averaged full-data laws by $\overline{\mathbb P}_+$ and
$\overline{\mathbb P}_-$.  The permutation lemma gives
\[
\operatorname{TV}\!\left(
\overline{\mathbb P}_\pm,
\lambda^{\otimes Q}\otimes(P^{(M)}_\pm)^{\otimes Q}
\right)
\le3\alpha_{Q,M}.
\]
Since adjoining the common factor $\lambda^{\otimes Q}$ does not change
total variation, the triangle inequality and
\eqref{eq:transfer-product-TV} yield
\[
\operatorname{TV}(\overline{\mathbb P}_+,\overline{\mathbb P}_-)
\le
6\alpha_{Q,M}+\frac{3}{64}
<\frac12.
\]

Applying \eqref{eq:transfer-bayes-reduction} with $b=a_M$ and then taking
the infimum over $\widehat\sigma$ gives
\[
\mathcal R^{\mathrm{obs}}_{Q,n}(beta,L)
\ge
\frac{a_M}{4}
\ge
\frac{Delta}{16}.
\]
Since this holds for every
$0<Delta<omega_{n,beta,L}(\varepsilon_Q)$,
this proves \eqref{eq:observed-transfer} with the stated universal constants.

label: lem:jackson
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Localized Jackson polynomial

title: Proof
body_md:
The key idea is to smooth the discontinuous sign function with a positive, normalized, finite-frequency Jackson kernel.  The resulting convolution is a bounded trigonometric polynomial that closely follows the sign function away from its jumps; evenness then converts it into an algebraic polynomial in $x=\cos\vartheta$.

Let $f(\vartheta):=\operatorname{sgn}(\cos\vartheta)$ on the circle $\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$, and choose an integer $r$ such that $2r-1>s$.  For $m\ge2$, define
\[
J_{m,r}(u)
:=c_{m,r}
\left(\frac{\sin(mu/2)}{\sin(u/2)}\right)^{2r},
\]
where the quotient is interpreted continuously at zero.  The constant $c_{m,r}$ is chosen to give normalization $\frac1{2\pi} \int_{-\pi}^{\pi} J_{m,r}(u)\,\,\mathrm d u=1$.

\emph{Kernel properties.}
Recall that the Fej\'er kernel satisfies
\[
F_m(u)
:=\frac1m\left(\frac{\sin(mu/2)}{\sin(u/2)}\right)^2
=
\sum_{k=-(m-1)}^{m-1}
\left(1-\frac{|k|}{m}\right)e^{iku}.
\]
Since $J_{m,r}=c_{m,r}m^rF_m^r$, it is nonnegative, even, and a trigonometric polynomial of degree $d:=r(m-1)$.

To determine its normalization scale, put $K_{m,r}^0(u):=(\sin(mu/2)/\sin(u/2))^{2r}$.  On $|u|\le1/m$, one has $K_{m,r}^0(u)\asymp_r m^{2r}$, while for $0<|u|\le\pi$, the inequalities $|\sin(u/2)|\ge|u|/\pi$ and $|\sin(mu/2)|\le1$ give $K_{m,r}^0(u)\lesssim_r|u|^{-2r}$.  Splitting the integral at $1/m$ therefore yields
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}K_{m,r}^0(u)\,\,\mathrm d u
\asymp_r m^{2r-1},
\qquad
c_{m,r}\asymp_r m^{-(2r-1)}.
\]
Only the resulting upper bound on $c_{m,r}$ is needed below.  We next bound the tail.  If $a\le1/m$, normalized total mass bounds it by one; if $a>1/m$, the preceding pointwise and normalization bounds give
\[
\frac1{2\pi}\int_{|u|\ge a}J_{m,r}(u)\,\,\mathrm d u
\lesssim_r
m^{-(2r-1)}\int_a^\pi u^{-2r}\,\,\mathrm d u
\lesssim_r
(ma)^{-(2r-1)}.
\]
Thus, for every $0<a\le\pi$,
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:jackson-tail}
\frac1{2\pi}\int_{|u|\ge a}J_{m,r}(u)\,\,\mathrm d u
\le
C_r\min\{1,(ma)^{-(2r-1)}\},
\qquad 0<a\le\pi.
\end{equation}

\emph{Finite-frequency smoothing.}
Define
\[
T_m(\vartheta)
:=
\frac1{2\pi}\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}
f(\vartheta-u)J_{m,r}(u)\,\,\mathrm d u.
\]
Since $J_{m,r}\ge0$ and has normalized mass one, $T_m(\vartheta)$ is a weighted average of values in $[-1,1]$, so $|T_m(\vartheta)|\le1$.  Write $J_{m,r}(u)=\sum_{|k|\le d}j_ke^{iku}$.  The convolution identity gives
\[
T_m(\vartheta)
=
\sum_{|k|\le d}j_k\widehat f(k)e^{ik\vartheta},
\]
where $\widehat f(k)$ is the $k$th Fourier coefficient of $f$.  Thus $T_m$ is a trigonometric polynomial of degree at most $d$.  Because both $f$ and $J_{m,r}$ are even, so is $T_m$, and hence it has a cosine expansion $T_m(\vartheta)=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^da_k\cos(k\vartheta)$.  If $\mathsf T_k$ denotes the $k$th Chebyshev polynomial, define $P(x):=a_0+\sum_{k=1}^da_k\mathsf T_k(x)$.  Then $P$ has degree at most $d$ and
\[
T_m(\vartheta)=P(\cos\vartheta),
\qquad
\norm P_{L_infinity[-1,1]}\le1.
\]

\emph{Localized approximation error.}
Let $a(\vartheta)$ denote the circular distance from $\vartheta$ to the nearest discontinuity of $f$, namely $\pi/2$ or $3\pi/2$.  Whenever $|u|<a(\vartheta)$, the values $f(\vartheta-u)$ and $f(\vartheta)$ agree.  Therefore \eqref{eq:jackson-tail} implies
\[
\begin{aligned}
|T_m(\vartheta)-f(\vartheta)|
&\le
\frac2{2\pi}\int_{|u|\ge a(\vartheta)}J_{m,r}(u)\,\,\mathrm d u\\
&\le
C_r\min\{1,(m a(\vartheta))^{-(2r-1)}\}.
\end{aligned}
\]
If $x=\cos\vartheta$, then $|x|=\sin a(\vartheta)\le a(\vartheta)$.  For $n\ge2r$, take $m=1+\lfloor n/r\rfloor$.  Then $d=r(m-1)\le n$ and $m\ge n/r$.  Since $2r-1>s$, the last display implies \eqref{eq:jackson-bound}, after enlarging the constant.  For the finitely many integers $1\le n<2r$, take $P_n\equiv0$ and enlarge $C_s$.

label: lem:weighted-sign
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Weighted $L_1$ approximation of a jump

title: Proof
body_md:
The upper bound follows from \cref{lem:jackson,lem:integrated-approx}, because $\mu_beta([-t,t])=t^beta$.

For the lower bound, we use only the inverse theorem of \citet[Theorem~9.1]{Kopotun}.  The power weight
$w_beta(x):=|x|^{beta-1}$
is the generalized-Jacobi weight with one designated point $z_1=0$ and exponent $beta-1>-1$, and belongs to the class treated there.  Fix an integer $r>beta$, which will be the order of the modulus, and a sufficiently large constant $A$.  Specializing Kopotun's theorem to $p=1$, and absorbing the normalization of $\mu_beta$ into the constant, gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:kopotun-inverse}
omega_\varphi^r(f,A,m^{-1})_{1,w_beta}
\le
C m^{-r}\sum_{k=1}^m k^{r-1}E_k(f)_{1,w_beta},
\end{equation}
Here $\norm{g}_{1,w_beta}:=\int_{-1}^1|g(x)|w_beta(x)\,\,\mathrm d x$, $E_k(f)_{1,w_beta}:=\inf_{P\in\Pi_k}\norm{f-P}_{1,w_beta}$, and $omega_\varphi^r(f,A,m^{-1})_{1,w_beta}$ is the complete weighted modulus of smoothness defined in \citet[Section~3]{Kopotun}.  The normalization of $\mu_beta$ gives $E_k(\operatorname{sgn})_{1,w_beta}=(2/beta)E_k(beta)$.  Kopotun uses $\Pi_k$ for polynomials of degree less than $k$, whereas our $\Pi_k$ contains polynomials of degree at most $k$; this one-degree shift only affects the constants.

For $f=\operatorname{sgn}$, the definition of the complete modulus simplifies substantially.  Its main-part finite-difference term is evaluated away from a neighborhood of zero and vanishes because $\operatorname{sgn}$ is constant on each remaining component.  Only the local best-approximation term remains:
\[
omega_\varphi^r(\operatorname{sgn},A,t)_{1,w_beta}
=
\inf_{P\in\Pi_{r-1}}
\int_{-b_t}^{b_t}|\operatorname{sgn}(x)-P(x)|\,|x|^{beta-1}\,\,\mathrm d x,
\qquad
b_t:=2A\rho(t,0)=2A(t+t^2),
\]
for all sufficiently small $t$. The zero polynomial gives an upper bound of order $t^beta$.  For the reverse bound, the interval $[-b_t,b_t]$ contains $[-2At,2At]$, and the substitution $x=tu$ gives
\[
\inf_{P\in\Pi_{r-1}}
\int_{-2At}^{2At}|\operatorname{sgn}(x)-P(x)|\,|x|^{beta-1}\,\,\mathrm d x
=
t^beta
\inf_{Q\in\Pi_{r-1}}
\int_{-2A}^{2A}|\operatorname{sgn}(u)-Q(u)|\,|u|^{beta-1}\,\,\mathrm d u.
\]
The last infimum is strictly positive: $\Pi_{r-1}$ is a finite-dimensional closed subspace of the weighted $L_1$ space, whereas $\operatorname{sgn}$ is not equal almost everywhere to a polynomial.  We have therefore shown that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:sign-complete-modulus}
omega_\varphi^r(\operatorname{sgn},A,t)_{1,w_beta}
\asymp
t^beta,
\qquad 0<t\le t_beta.
\end{equation}
Together, \eqref{eq:kopotun-inverse} and \eqref{eq:sign-complete-modulus} give a lower bound of order $m^{-beta}$ on a weighted average of $E_1(beta),\ldots,E_m(beta)$ for all sufficiently large $m$.  It remains to extract a pointwise lower bound for $E_n(beta)$.

Write $E_k:=E_k(beta)$.  By the upper bound already established, $E_k\lesssim k^{-beta}$.  Apply \eqref{eq:kopotun-inverse} with $m=Mn$, where $M\ge2$ is a fixed integer to be chosen.  By \eqref{eq:sign-complete-modulus},
\[
c(Mn)^{-beta}
\le
C(Mn)^{-r}\sum_{k=1}^{Mn}k^{r-1}E_k.
\]
Split the sum at $n$.  Using $E_k\lesssim k^{-beta}$ on the first part and monotonicity $E_k\le E_n$ for $k\ge n$ on the second gives
\[
\sum_{k=1}^{n}k^{r-1}E_k
\lesssim n^{r-beta},
\qquad
\sum_{k=n+1}^{Mn}k^{r-1}E_k
\lesssim (Mn)^rE_n.
\]
Consequently,
\[
cM^{-beta}n^{-beta}
\le
C_3M^{-r}n^{-beta}+C_4E_n.
\]
Since $r>beta$, choose the fixed $M$ large enough that $C_3M^{-r}\le(c/2)M^{-beta}$.  The first term on the right can then be absorbed into the left,
giving
$E_n\gtrsim n^{-beta}$.  Decreasing the implicit constant handles the finitely many small values of $n$ not covered by \eqref{eq:sign-complete-modulus}.

label: lem:duality-moment-pair
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: $L_1$ duality produces a moment-canceling family

title: Proof
body_md:
The polynomial-approximation error admits a dual certificate $h_m$ that annihilates every polynomial in $\Pi_m$ while being maximally correlated with $\operatorname{sgn}$.  Perturbing the reference measure in the directions $\pm h_m$ will then produce moment-matched distributions with oppositely separated targets.

Let $f:=\operatorname{sgn}$ and use the dual pairing
\[
\langle g,h\rangle
:=
\int g(x)h(x)\,\,\mathrm d\mu_beta(x),
\qquad
g\in L_1(\mu_beta),\quad h\in L_infinity(\mu_beta).
\]
Since $E_m(beta)$ is the $L_1$ distance from $f$ to the subspace $\Pi_m$, it has the following dual representation; see \cref{rem:l1-duality}.
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:l1-duality}
E_m(beta)
=
\max_{\substack{h\in L_infinity(\mu_beta),\ \norm h_infinity\le1\\
\langle P,h\rangle=0\ \text{for every }P\in\Pi_m}}
\langle f,h\rangle.
\end{equation}
The maximum is attained by weak-$^*$ compactness.  We may choose a maximizer that is odd.  Indeed, if $h$ is feasible, then
\[
h_{\mathrm{odd}}(x):=\frac{h(x)-h(-x)}2
\]
is feasible, has $L_infinity$ norm at most one, and has the same objective value because $\mu_beta$ is symmetric, $\Pi_m$ is reflection invariant, and $\operatorname{sgn}$ is odd.

Let $h_m$ be such an odd maximizer and define $G_{m,\pm}$ by \eqref{eq:raw-dual-pair}.  These measures are nonnegative because $\norm{h_m}_infinity\le1$.  Orthogonality to the constant polynomial makes their total masses one; orthogonality to $x^j$, $j=0,\dots,m$, makes their moments equal.  Moreover,
\[
G_{m,\pm}([-t,t])
\le
2\mu_beta([-t,t])
=
2t^beta.
\]
Oddness gives $G_{m,-}=G_{m,+}^\dagger$.  Finally, symmetry of $\mu_beta$ gives $\int\operatorname{sgn}\,\,\mathrm d\mu_beta=0$, so \eqref{eq:l1-duality} gives
\[
theta(G_{m,+})
=
\int\operatorname{sgn}(x)h_m(x)\,\,\mathrm d\mu_beta(x)
=
E_m(beta),
\]
and reflection gives the target of $G_{m,-}$.

It remains to verify the claims for the adjusted pair.  For every $0<t<1$, the outer atoms do not contribute and
\[
H_{m,\pm}([-t,t])
\le
2\rho_Lt^beta
\le
Lt^beta;
\]
at $t=1$, the required inequality is $1\le L$.  Thus $H_{m,\pm}\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}$.  Adding the same symmetric measure to the two raw alternatives preserves their moment matching, and symmetry of $H_0$ together with reflection of the raw pair gives $H_{m,-}=H_{m,+}^\dagger$.  Finally, $theta(H_0)=0$, so
\[
theta(H_{m,+})
=-theta(H_{m,-})
=\rho_LE_m(beta).
\]
head: environment

label: rem:l1-duality
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:l1-duality}
Identity~\eqref{eq:l1-duality} is the infinite-dimensional analogue of linear-programming duality.  Indeed, put $E:=\inf_{P\in\Pi_m}\norm{f-P}_{L_1(\mu_beta)}$.  For every feasible $h$ and every $P\in\Pi_m$,
\[
\langle f,h\rangle
=
\langle f-P,h\rangle
\le
\norm{f-P}_{L_1(\mu_beta)},
\]
so the dual value is at most $E$.  Hahn--Banach supplies a norm-one functional on $L_1(\mu_beta)$ that annihilates $\Pi_m$ and takes the value $E$ at $f$.  Identifying $L_1(\mu_beta)^*$ with $L_infinity(\mu_beta)$ represents this functional by a feasible $h$ attaining equality, and hence establishes strong duality.

\[
\mathbb P_\pm

(K_nH_{n,\pm})^{\otimes Q}
\]
denote the laws of the full $Q$-question experiment.  Moment equivalence gives $\mathbb P_+=\mathbb P_-$.  Hence, for every decision rule $\widehat\sigma$,
\begin{align*}
\sup_{G\in\mathcal G_{beta,L}}
\mathbb E_G\mathcal L_G(\widehat\sigma)
&\ge
\frac{\rho_LE_n(beta)}2
\left[
\mathbb P_+(\widehat\sigma=-1)
+
\mathbb P_-(\widehat\sigma=+1)
\right]\\
&=
\frac{\rho_LE_n(beta)}2.
\end{align*}
The equality uses $\mathbb P_+=\mathbb P_-$ and $\widehat\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}$.  The prefactor $\rho_LE_n(beta)$ is the cost of a wrong decision under either alternative, since $|theta(H_{n,\pm})|=\rho_LE_n(beta)$.  Taking the infimum over $\widehat\sigma$ gives $\mathcal R^{\mathrm{dec}}_{Q,n}(beta,L)\gtrsim_{beta,L}n^{-beta}$, independently of $Q$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Expand $P(z)=c_0+\sum_{j=1}^dc_jT_j(z)$ in Chebyshev polynomials.  The cosine coefficient formula and $\norm P_infinity\le1$ give $|c_0|\le1$ and $|c_j|\le2$ for $j\ge1$.  Let $L_j$ be the sum of the absolute values of the monomial coefficients of $T_j$.  The recurrence $T_{j+1}(z)=2zT_j(z)-T_{j-1}(z)$ gives $L_{j+1}\le2L_j+L_{j-1}$; since $L_0=L_1=1$, it follows that $L_j\le C(1+\sqrt2)^j$.  After substituting $z=2p-1$, each monomial $z^\ell$ has absolute coefficient sum $3^\ell$, so the corresponding sum for $T_j(2p-1)$ is at most $C\{3(1+\sqrt2)\}^j$.

Write $P(2p-1)=\sum_{j=0}^d r_jp^j$, so the $r_j$ are its coefficients in the ordinary power basis.  The preceding bounds and a geometric sum give $\sum_{j=0}^d|r_j|\le C_0B_0^d$, with $B_0=7.5>3(1+\sqrt2)$.

For any $n\ge d$, the identity $p^j=\sum_{k=j}^n\frac{\binom kj}{\binom nj}b_{k,n}(p)$ gives the degree-$n$ Bernstein coefficients directly:
\[
a_k(P)=\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,d)}r_j\frac{\binom kj}{\binom nj},
\qquad 0\le k\le n.
\]
Every ratio in this sum lies in $[0,1]$, so $|a_k(P)|\le\sum_{j=0}^d|r_j|\le C_0B_0^d$.

title: Proof
body_md:
The operator $D_n=T_nT_n^*$ is self-adjoint and positive.  It also preserves each polynomial space $\Pi_j$.  Indeed, beta integration gives
\[
(T_n^*u^j)(k)
=
\frac{(n+1)!}{(n+j+1)!}(k+1)(k+2)\cdots(k+j),
\]
which is a degree-$j$ polynomial in $k$.  Averaging this polynomial under $k\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$ shows that $D_nu^j\in\Pi_j$ and that its leading coefficient is
\[
\lambda_{j,n}
=
\frac{n!(n+1)!}{(n-j)!(n+j+1)!}.
\]
Here we use the fact that the expectation of a monic degree-$j$ polynomial in a $\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)$ variable has leading coefficient $n!/(n-j)!$ as a polynomial in $p$.

For $j=0$, the claim follows directly from $D_n1=1$.  For $j\ge1$, because $L_0,\dots,L_j$ are obtained by orthogonalizing $1,u,\dots,u^j$,
\[
\Pi_j
=
\Pi_{j-1}\oplus\operatorname{span}\{L_j\}.
\]
Now $D_nL_j\in\Pi_j$ by degree preservation.  For every $q\in\Pi_{j-1}$, self-adjointness and degree preservation give
\[
\left\langleD_nL_j,q\right\rangle_{L_2}
=
\left\langleL_j,D_nq\right\rangle_{L_2}
=0,
\]
because $D_nq\in\Pi_{j-1}$ and $L_j\perp\Pi_{j-1}$.  Hence $D_nL_j$ lies in the one-dimensional space $\Pi_j\cap\Pi_{j-1}^\perp=\operatorname{span}\{L_j\}$.  Comparing leading coefficients proves \eqref{eq:durrmeyer-eigen}.

Define
$
v_j=\lambda_{j,n}^{-1/2}T_n^*L_j.
$
Then
\[
\left\langlev_i,v_j\right\rangle_{\nu_n}
=
\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{i,n}\lambda_{j,n}}}
\left\langleL_i,D_nL_j\right\rangle_{L_2}
=\mathbf 1\{i=j\},
\]
and
$
T_nv_j=\sqrt{\lambda_{j,n}}L_j.
$
There are $n+1$ orthonormal vectors $v_j$ in the $(n+1)$-dimensional space $\mathsf H_n$, so they form a basis.  Thus $(v_j,L_j,\sqrt{\lambda_{j,n}})$ is a singular system and \eqref{eq:durrmeyer-svd} follows.

If $P\in\Pi_d$, write $\widetilde P=\sum_{j=0}^dc_jL_j$.  Since $T_na(P)=\widetilde P$, comparison of the Legendre coefficients in \eqref{eq:durrmeyer-svd} gives
\[
\left\langlea(P),v_j\right\rangle_{\nu_n}
=
\begin{cases}
c_j/\sqrt{\lambda_{j,n}},&0\le j\le d,\\
0,&d<j\le n.
\end{cases}
\]
Consequently,
\[
a(P)=\sum_{j=0}^d\frac{c_j}{\sqrt{\lambda_{j,n}}}v_j.
\]
Parseval's identity in $\mathsf H_n$ now gives
\[
\frac1{n+1}\sum_{k=0}^na_k(P)^2
=
\norm{a(P)}_{\nu_n}^2
=
\sum_{j=0}^d\frac{c_j^2}{\lambda_{j,n}},
\]
which proves \eqref{eq:coefficient-spectral}.  Since $j\mapsto\lambda_{j,n}$ is decreasing, Parseval in $L_2[0,1]$ also gives
\[
\norm{a(P)}_{\nu_n}
\le
\kappa_{d,n}
\left(\sum_{j=0}^dc_j^2\right)^{1/2}
=
\kappa_{d,n}\norm{\widetilde P}_{L_2[0,1]}.
\]
Finally,
\[
\max_k|a_k(P)|
\le
\sqrt{\sum_{k=0}^na_k(P)^2}
=
\sqrt{n+1}\norm{a(P)}_{\nu_n}.
\]
Applying the same bound to the maximum and minimum proves \eqref{eq:range-spectral}.

name: Adjoint tail identity for integrable perturbations

title: Proof
body_md:
Define the coefficient vector $T_n^*g$ algebraically by
\[
(T_n^*g)(k)=(n+1)u_k.
\]
The vectors $v_0,\dots,v_n$ in \cref{app:durrmeyer} form an orthonormal basis of $(\mathbb R^{n+1},\nu_n)$ and satisfy $T_nv_j=\sqrt{\lambda_{j,n}}L_j$.  Although $g$ need not belong to $L_2$, every integral below is finite because $g\in L_1$ and $L_j$ is bounded.  Hence
\[
\langle T_n^*g,v_j\rangle_{\nu_n}
=
\int_0^1g(p)(T_nv_j)(p)\,\,\mathrm d p
=
\sqrt{\lambda_{j,n}}
\int_0^1g(p)L_j(p)\,\,\mathrm d p.
\]
Parseval in the finite-dimensional coefficient space gives \eqref{eq:adjoint-tail-identity}, because
\[
\|T_n^*g\|_{\nu_n}^2
=
\frac1{n+1}\sum_{k=0}^n(n+1)^2u_k^2
=(n+1)\sum_{k=0}^nu_k^2.
\]

label: eq:spectral-pair-target
title: Proof
body_md:
Let $h_d$, $G_{d,\pm}$, and $H_{d,\pm}$ be, respectively, the degree-$d$ dual certificate, raw alternatives, and margin-adjusted alternatives supplied by \cref{lem:duality-moment-pair}.  By \cref{eq:adjusted-dual-target,lem:weighted-sign},
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:spectral-pair-target}
|theta(H_{d,+})-theta(H_{d,-})|
=2\rho_LE_d(beta)
\ge c_{beta,L}d^{-beta}.
\end{equation}

We now bound the Hellinger distance between their count laws.  Write $p=(1+z)/2$.  Under this transformation, $\mu_beta$ has density
\[
w_beta(p)=beta|2p-1|^{beta-1},
\qquad 0<p<1,
\]
with respect to Lebesgue measure.  Put
\[
g_d(p):=h_d(2p-1)w_beta(p),
\]
and define
\[
q_0(k):=\int_0^1b_{k,n}(p)w_beta(p)\,\,\mathrm d p,
\qquad
u_d(k):=\int_0^1b_{k,n}(p)g_d(p)\,\,\mathrm d p.
\]
Then
\[
K_nG_{d,+}=q_0+u_d,
\qquad
K_nG_{d,-}=q_0-u_d.
\]
If $r_0:=K_nH_0$ and $m_0:=\rho_Lq_0+(1-\rho_L)r_0$, the final pair has probability mass functions
\[
P_{d,+}:=K_nH_{d,+}=m_0+\rho_Lu_d,
\qquad
P_{d,-}:=K_nH_{d,-}=m_0-\rho_Lu_d.
\]
Because $m_0\ge\rho_Lq_0$ coordinatewise,
\begin{align}
 h^2(P_{d,+},P_{d,-})
&=
\sum_{k=0}^n
\left(\sqrt{m_0(k)+\rho_Lu_d(k)}-
\sqrt{m_0(k)-\rho_Lu_d(k)}\right)^2\notag\\
&\le
2\rho_L^2\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{u_d(k)^2}{m_0(k)}
\le
2\rho_L\sum_{k=0}^n\frac{u_d(k)^2}{q_0(k)}.
\label{eq:hellinger-baseline}
\end{align}
For $0<beta\le1$, $w_beta(p)\gebeta$ for almost every $p\in(0,1)$, and
$
\int_0^1b_{k,n}(p)\,\,\mathrm d p=\frac1{n+1}.
$
Thus
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:q0-lower}
q_0(k)\ge\fracbeta{n+1}.
\end{equation}
Combining \eqref{eq:hellinger-baseline} and \eqref{eq:q0-lower} gives
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:hellinger-adjoint}
h^2(P_{d,+},P_{d,-})
\le
\frac{2\rho_L(n+1)}beta
\sum_{k=0}^nu_d(k)^2
=
\frac{2\rho_L}beta
\|T_n^*g_d\|_{\nu_n}^2.
\end{equation}

The cancellation in \eqref{eq:hm-properties} removes the first $d$ singular modes.  Indeed, $L_j((1+z)/2)$ is a polynomial of degree $j$ in $z$, so
\[
\int_0^1g_d(p)L_j(p)\,\,\mathrm d p=0,
\qquad j=0,\dots,d.
\]
By \cref{lem:adjoint-tail} and the monotonicity of $j\mapsto\lambda_{j,n}$,
\begin{align*}
\|T_n^*g_d\|_{\nu_n}^2
&=
\sum_{j=d+1}^n
\lambda_{j,n}
\left(\int_0^1g_d(p)L_j(p)\,\,\mathrm d p\right)^2\\
&\le
\lambda_{d+1,n}
\sum_{j=d+1}^n
\left(\int_0^1g_d(p)L_j(p)\,\,\mathrm d p\right)^2.
\end{align*}
Since $\|g_d\|_1\le1$ and the orthonormal shifted Legendre polynomial satisfies $\|L_j\|_infinity=\sqrt{2j+1}$,
\[
\left|\int_0^1g_d(p)L_j(p)\,\,\mathrm d p\right|
\le\sqrt{2j+1}.
\]
Therefore
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:L1-tail}
\|T_n^*g_d\|_{\nu_n}^2
\le
\lambda_{d+1,n}
\sum_{j=0}^n(2j+1)
=
\lambda_{d+1,n}(n+1)^2.
\end{equation}
Equations \eqref{eq:hellinger-adjoint} and \eqref{eq:L1-tail} imply
\[
h(P_{d,+},P_{d,-})
\le
C_{beta,L}
\frac{n+1}{\kappa_{d+1,n}}.
\]
Together with \eqref{eq:spectral-pair-target}, this proves \eqref{eq:spectral-modulus-lower}.

If $beta>1/2$, then $g_d\in L_2[0,1]$ and
$
\|g_d\|_2^2
\le
\int_0^1w_beta(p)^2\,\,\mathrm d p
=
\frac{beta^2}{2beta-1}.
$
Bessel's inequality replaces \eqref{eq:L1-tail} by
\[
\|T_n^*g_d\|_{\nu_n}^2
\le
\lambda_{d+1,n}\|g_d\|_2^2
\le
C_beta\lambda_{d+1,n}.
\]
Substitution into \eqref{eq:hellinger-adjoint} proves \eqref{eq:spectral-modulus-lower-L2}.

A_{beta,L}(n+1)\sqrt Q.

(n\Lambda_{Q,n})^{-beta/2}.

\[
\frac{\sqrt{n+1}\,\kappa_{d,n}}{\sqrt Q}
\lesssim
\frac{\sqrt n\,e^{x_{Q,n}/4}}
{n^{(beta+1)/2}e^{x_{Q,n}/2}}
=
n^{-beta/2}e^{-x_{Q,n}/4}.
\]
Since $e^{-x/4}\le C_beta x^{-beta/2}$ for $x\ge1$, the stochastic term has the same stated order, proving \eqref{eq:intermediate-upper}.
